lessons.title: Cell structures and what they do
lessons.text:
## Cell structures and what they do
LV: GCSE · Foundation
S: Plant, animal and bacterial cells are built from a small set of parts, and each part has a structure that suits one job. Knowing what each part does lets you explain how a cell stays alive, makes food or releases energy.
PRE: Animal cells
PRE: Plant cells
O: Name the main structures of animal, plant and bacterial cells and state the job of each
O: Explain how the nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondria and chloroplasts are suited to their jobs
O: Identify a cell as animal, plant or bacterial from the structures it contains
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.2.a @1,2,3
T: Mitochondrion | A structure in the cytoplasm that holds the enzymes for aerobic respiration, where most of a cell's energy is released (plural: mitochondria)
T: Chloroplast | A structure in some plant cells that contains chlorophyll to absorb light and the enzymes needed for photosynthesis
T: Plasmid | A small ring of DNA found in some bacterial cells, in addition to the main loop of DNA
T: Cell sap | The liquid that fills the permanent vacuole of a plant cell
H: Parts found in animal cells
P: Most animal cells contain five main parts. Plant cells contain all five as well, so these are the parts the two kinds of cell share.
- **Nucleus**: holds the cell's DNA. Because DNA carries the instructions for the cell, the nucleus directs what the cell does. It has its own membrane around it, and having a nucleus enclosed like this is what makes a cell eukaryotic.
- **Cytoplasm**: a jelly-like substance holding dissolved nutrients and the cell's other structures. Many of the cell's chemical reactions happen here.
- **Cell membrane**: a thin layer around the cell that is selective, so it controls which substances enter and leave.
- **Mitochondria**: contain the enzymes for aerobic respiration, the process that releases most of the cell's energy. They make ATP, the molecule cells use to carry that energy.
- **Ribosomes**: tiny structures where proteins are made. They are so small that only an electron microscope shows them.
D: bio-animal-cell
P: Animal cells may also have small vacuoles that come and go, used for storing or moving substances.
H: Extra parts in plant cells
- **Cell wall**: a layer of cellulose outside the membrane that strengthens the cell. Algal cells have a cellulose wall too.
- **Chloroplasts**: contain green chlorophyll, which absorbs light, and the enzymes for photosynthesis. Inside are stacks of membranes called thylakoids. Chloroplasts also have their own DNA and ribosomes.
- **Permanent vacuole**: a large space filled with cell sap, which helps keep the cell firm (turgid).
D: bio-plant-cell
P: Not every plant cell has chloroplasts, but plant cells often do. The diagrams include some extra structures; for this topic, focus on the parts named here.
K: Each structure matches its job: the nucleus holds the DNA that directs the cell, the membrane controls what passes in and out, mitochondria hold the enzymes for aerobic respiration, and chloroplasts hold chlorophyll and the enzymes for photosynthesis.
H: Bacterial cells
P: Bacterial cells are much smaller than plant or animal cells and have no nucleus. Their DNA is a single loop lying in the cytoplasm, and many also carry one or more **plasmids**, small extra rings of DNA. Like plant cells, bacteria have a cell wall outside the membrane.
X: A cell has a cell wall, a large vacuole and chloroplasts, and its DNA is inside a nucleus. Identify it.
> A nucleus means the cell is eukaryotic, so it is not a bacterium.
> A cell wall rules out an animal cell.
> Chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole are plant features, so it is a plant cell.
!: Thinking only plant cells have mitochondria, or that chloroplasts replace them. Plant and animal cells both respire, so both have mitochondria; plant cells may have chloroplasts as well.
!: Mixing up the cell wall and the cell membrane. The wall is a rigid cellulose layer on the outside; the membrane is thin and selective, and it is the membrane that controls what enters.
Q: What is the job of the nucleus? | It holds the cell's DNA, and so directs the cell's activities.
Q: Why are mitochondria important to a cell? | They hold the enzymes for aerobic respiration, which releases most of the cell's energy.
Q: What do chloroplasts contain that lets them carry out photosynthesis? | Chlorophyll, which absorbs light, and the enzymes needed for photosynthesis.
Q: What does the cell membrane do? | It is selective: it controls which substances move into and out of the cell.
Q: How is DNA arranged in a bacterial cell? | As a single loop in the cytoplasm, often with small extra rings called plasmids; there is no nucleus.
Q: What does the cell wall of a plant cell do? | Made of cellulose, it strengthens the cell.
M1@1: In which structure are proteins made? | Ribosomes | Mitochondria | Chloroplasts | Nucleus | Proteins are made on ribosomes, which are so small that they can only be seen with an electron microscope.
M1@1: Which structure holds the enzymes for aerobic respiration? | Mitochondria | Ribosomes | Chloroplasts | Vacuole | Mitochondria hold the enzymes for aerobic respiration, which releases most of the energy a cell needs.
M2@2: A cell takes in glucose but keeps its proteins inside. Which structure controls this? | The cell membrane | The cellulose wall | The nuclear membrane | The cytoplasm | The membrane is selective and controls movement in and out; the cellulose wall strengthens the cell but does not select substances.
M2@2: Why can a leaf cell make its own food while an animal cell cannot? | Its chloroplasts hold chlorophyll and enzymes to make food using light | Its mitochondria make food from light instead of releasing energy | Its nucleus holds extra DNA that animal cells do not have | Its cell wall absorbs light and passes it into the cytoplasm | Photosynthesis needs chlorophyll to absorb light and the right enzymes, and both are found in chloroplasts.
M3@2,3: A student says plant cells have chloroplasts instead of mitochondria. Which reply is correct? | Plant cells respire too, so they need mitochondria as well | Correct, because chloroplasts release all the energy plants need | Correct for leaves, but every plant cell in the dark has mitochondria | Wrong, because plant cells have mitochondria but no chloroplasts | Plant and animal cells both carry out aerobic respiration, so both have mitochondria; many plant cells also have chloroplasts.
M3@3: A cell has a cell wall, a single loop of DNA and plasmids, but no nucleus. What is it? | A bacterial cell | A plant leaf cell | An animal cell | An algal cell | Without a nucleus the cell cannot be plant, animal or algal; a DNA loop with plasmids and a wall is the bacterial pattern.
SUM: The nucleus holds the DNA and so directs the cell, and the cytoplasm is where many reactions happen.
SUM: The cell membrane is selective, controlling which substances enter and leave the cell.
SUM: Mitochondria hold the enzymes for aerobic respiration, and ribosomes are where proteins are made.
SUM: Plant cells may add a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a permanent vacuole of cell sap.
SUM: Bacterial cells have no nucleus; their DNA is one loop, often with plasmids, inside a cell wall.

lessons.title: Estimating the sizes of cell parts
lessons.text:
## Estimating the sizes of cell parts
LV: GCSE · Foundation
S: Cells and the structures inside them are far too small to measure with a ruler, so biologists use small units, standard form and sensible rough estimates. These skills let you compare structures and check whether a calculated size makes sense.
PRE: Units and conversions
PRE: Scientific notation
PRE: Cell structures and what they do
O: Convert lengths between millimetres, micrometres and nanometres and write them in standard form
O: Calculate magnification and relative size after putting both lengths in the same unit
O: Make rough estimates of size and decide when an estimate is good enough for a comparison
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.2.e @1,2,3
T: Micrometre | One thousandth of a millimetre, or 1 × 10^{-6} metres; the usual unit for cells
T: Nanometre | 1 × 10^{-9} metres; used for very small structures such as ribosomes and viruses
T: Order of magnitude | A difference in size expressed as a factor of ten
T: Standard form | A way of writing a number as A × 10^{n}, where A is between 1 and 10
T: Magnification | How many times larger an image is than the real object
H: Units for small things
P: A typical animal cell is about 0.01 to 0.05 mm across, and a plant cell about 0.01 to 0.10 mm. Your eye can only pick out detail down to about 0.05 mm, which is why most cells need a microscope.
P: Millimetres give awkward decimals at this scale, so cells are measured in **micrometres** (µm): there are 1000 micrometres in a millimetre. Ribosomes and viruses are smaller still and are measured in **nanometres** (nm).
- centi means one hundredth (10^{-2}), as in centimetre
- milli means one thousandth (10^{-3}), as in millimetre
- micro means one millionth (10^{-6}), as in micrometre
- nano means one thousand-millionth (10^{-9}), as in nanometre
X: Convert 70 µm to millimetres and write it in standard form.
> There are 1000 µm in 1 mm, so divide by 1000: 70 ÷ 1000 = 0.07 mm.
> In standard form, 0.07 mm is 7 × 10^{-2} mm.
H: Magnification and relative size
E: magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object :: both sizes must be in the same unit first
P: To compare two structures, convert both sizes to one unit, then divide the larger by the smaller. The answer tells you how many times bigger one is. Each factor of ten is one **order of magnitude**.
X: A drawing shows a cheek cell 35 mm wide. The real cell is 70 µm wide. Find the magnification.
> Convert the real size to millimetres: 70 ÷ 1000 = 0.07 mm.
> Divide image size by real size: 35 ÷ 0.07 = 500.
> The magnification is ×500, or 5 × 10^{2} in standard form.
X: A leaf cell is 70 µm long and a red blood cell is 7 µm across. A cheek cell is 70 µm and a bacterium is 0.5 µm. Compare each pair.
> Both pairs are already in micrometres, so no conversion is needed.
> Leaf cell and red blood cell: 70 ÷ 7 = 10, so the leaf cell is 10 times longer, one order of magnitude.
> Cheek cell and bacterium: 70 ÷ 0.5 = 140, so the cheek cell is about 140 times wider, roughly two orders of magnitude (140 is closest to 10^{2}).
!: Dividing sizes in different units, such as 35 mm by 70 µm. Convert both to the same unit before you divide, or the answer will be wrong by a factor of 1000.
H: When a rough estimate is enough
P: Cell sizes vary, so a rough figure is often all you need. If the question is which structure is bigger, or by about how many times, rounding to a simple number is good enough. An estimate also lets you check a calculation: if a "cell" works out at several millimetres, a unit has gone wrong.
P: You can estimate area in the same way, by judging roughly how much of a drawing or micrograph a structure covers. Comparing your own drawing with a micrograph or photograph of the same cells is a good check.
K: Put both sizes into one unit before dividing; use exact figures for calculations, and rough estimates when you only need to know which is bigger or by roughly how many times.
Q: How many micrometres are in one millimetre? | 1000.
Q: How do you find how many times bigger one structure is than another? | Convert both sizes to the same unit, then divide the larger size by the smaller.
Q: What is the formula for magnification? | Magnification equals the size of the image divided by the size of the real object.
Q: What is one order of magnitude? | A difference in size by a factor of ten.
Q: Which unit suits ribosomes and viruses? | Nanometres (nm), each 1 × 10^{-9} metres.
M1@1: Which unit is most sensible for measuring a ribosome? | Nanometres | Micrometres | Millimetres | Centimetres | Ribosomes are far smaller than cells, which are measured in micrometres, so nanometres give sensible numbers.
M1@1: What is 0.05 mm in micrometres? | 50 µm | 5 µm | 500 µm | 0.00005 µm | There are 1000 micrometres in a millimetre, so multiply by 1000: 0.05 × 1000 = 50.
M2@2: A drawing of a cell is 20 mm wide and the real cell is 0.04 mm wide. What is the magnification? | ×500 | ×50 | ×0.002 | ×5000 | Magnification is image size divided by real size, both in mm: 20 ÷ 0.04 = 500.
M2@2: A drawing is 30 mm wide and the real cell is 60 µm wide. A student divides 30 by 60 and gets 0.5. What went wrong? | The sizes were in different units, so 60 µm must become 0.06 mm first | The real size should have been divided by the image size, not the reverse | The answer must be given in standard form, so it should read 5 × 10^{-1} | Nothing went wrong, because magnification can be less than one for cells | Converting 60 µm to 0.06 mm gives 30 ÷ 0.06 = 500, so the magnification is ×500.
M3@2,3: A cheek cell is 70 µm across and a bacterium is 0.5 µm. About how many times wider is the cheek cell? | About 140 times | About 35 times | About 14 times | About 1400 times | Both sizes are in micrometres, so divide: 70 ÷ 0.5 = 140, roughly two orders of magnitude.
M3@3: When is a rough estimate good enough instead of an exact measurement? | When you only need to know which structure is larger, or by roughly how much | When you calibrate a scale and need the exact length of each division | Never, because a size in biology must always be exact to the micrometre | Only when the two sizes are in different units and cannot be compared | Estimates suit comparisons of relative size or area; exact values are needed for calculations such as calibration.
SUM: Cells are measured in micrometres (one thousandth of a millimetre), and ribosomes and viruses in nanometres.
SUM: Magnification equals image size divided by real size, with both in the same unit.
SUM: To compare two structures, convert to one unit and divide; each factor of ten is one order of magnitude.
SUM: A rough estimate is good enough when you only need to know which structure is bigger, or by about how much.

lessons.title: Required practical 1: viewing cells with a light microscope
lessons.text:
## Required practical 1: viewing cells with a light microscope
LV: GCSE · Foundation
S: Looking at real plant and animal cells under a light microscope, then drawing and labelling them with a magnification, is AQA's first required practical. It builds the skills of preparing slides, focusing and measuring that exam questions test.
PRE: Cell structures and what they do
PRE: Estimating the sizes of cell parts
O: Prepare a slide and focus a light microscope, moving from low to high power
O: Make a clearly labelled drawing of plant or animal cells that includes a magnification scale
O: Measure cells using an eyepiece graticule calibrated with a stage micrometer
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.2.RP1 @1,2,3
T: Resolution | The ability to see two points that are close together as separate; higher resolution shows more detail
T: Eyepiece graticule | A scale inside the eyepiece, calibrated against a stage micrometer, used to measure cells
T: Stage micrometer | A slide with an accurate scale, used to work out the length of one eyepiece graticule division
H: Preparing and focusing
P: Common specimens are onion epidermis for plant cells and cheek cells for animal cells. The specimen must be thin so that light can pass through it.
- Place the thin specimen on a slide and add a stain so the cell parts show up more clearly.
- Lower a coverslip gently over it, so that no air bubbles are trapped.
- Start with the low-power objective, such as ×10.
- Focus with the coarse focus first, then sharpen the image with the fine focus.
- Then switch to the high-power objective, such as ×40, and refocus with the fine focus.
E: total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification :: a ×10 eyepiece with a ×40 objective gives ×400
X: A ×10 eyepiece is used with the ×10 and then the ×40 objective. Find the total magnification for each.
> Low power: 10 × 10 = 100, so ×100.
> High power: 10 × 40 = 400, so ×400.
DNEED: A labelled light microscope showing the eyepiece, objective lenses, stage with slide and coverslip, coarse and fine focus, and light source.
H: Drawing and labelling
- A **low-power plan** shows the regions of the tissue, without single cells drawn in detail.
- A **high-power drawing** shows the detail of one cell.
- Label every drawing, using straight label lines that touch the structure.
- Include a magnification scale, such as the total magnification you used.
K: Examiners look for full labels and a magnification scale on every drawing.
!: Sources differ on mitochondria: one revision guide says a light microscope shows them without detail, while AQA states only that electron microscopes show more detail. Label only the structures you can clearly see.
!: Thinking magnification and resolution are the same thing. Magnification makes the image bigger; resolution decides how much fine detail shows, and so limits how much magnification is useful.
H: Measuring with a graticule
P: The eyepiece graticule has no units of its own, so it is calibrated with a stage micrometer for each objective. Because each objective enlarges by a different amount, one graticule division covers a different real length at each one.
X: At high power, 250 µm on the stage micrometer lines up with 51 graticule divisions. A cell spans 12 divisions. How wide is it?
> Length of one division: 250 ÷ 51 gives about 4.9 µm.
> Cell width: 12 × 4.9 = 58.8, so the cell is about 59 µm wide.
H: How far a light microscope can go
P: A light microscope magnifies up to about ×1500 and resolves detail down to about 0.2 µm. A transmission electron microscope can magnify about a million times and resolve detail smaller than 1 nm, which is why electron microscopes revealed many more structures inside cells, including ribosomes.
SAFE: Do not use over-bright illumination through the eyepiece; avoid skin contact with stains and wash off any spills; handle glass slides and coverslips carefully and report breakages; take care with sharp mounted needles.
Q: Which objective should you use first? | The low-power objective, such as ×10, before moving to high power.
Q: Why lower the coverslip gently? | To avoid trapping air bubbles over the specimen.
Q: Why is a stain added to the specimen? | To increase contrast, so cell parts are easier to see.
Q: What is the difference between a low-power plan and a high-power drawing? | A low-power plan shows the regions of a tissue; a high-power drawing shows the detail of one cell.
Q: Why must the graticule be calibrated for each objective? | Each objective enlarges differently, so one division stands for a different real length at each.
M1@1: Why is the coverslip lowered gently onto the specimen? | To avoid trapping air bubbles | To spread the stain evenly | To push the cells into one layer | To stop the stain from soaking in | Air bubbles look like dark rings and hide the cells, so the coverslip is lowered slowly from one side.
M1@1: Which objective lens should you focus with first? | The low-power lens, such as ×10 | The high-power lens, such as ×40 | The most powerful lens available | Any lens, then add the stain | Start on low power with coarse then fine focus; it is easier to find the specimen before moving to high power.
SEQ2@1: Put these steps in order to view onion cells. | Place a thin specimen on the slide and add stain ; Lower the coverslip gently ; Focus with the low-power objective using coarse then fine focus ; Switch to the high-power objective and refocus with fine focus | The specimen is prepared and covered first, then found on low power before the view is enlarged on high power.
M2@2: Which drawing would gain full marks in the required practical? | Labelled cells with a magnification scale | Shaded cells with a magnification scale | Labelled cells with no magnification | A traced photo of cells, with labels | Examiners reward clear labels and a magnification scale on drawings of the cells you actually observed.
M2@3: One graticule division is 2.5 µm at high power. A cell spans 20 divisions. How wide is it? | 50 µm | 20 µm | 8 µm | 500 µm | Multiply the number of divisions by the length of one division: 20 × 2.5 = 50, so the cell is 50 µm wide.
M3@3: Why must the graticule be recalibrated after changing to a different objective? | Each division now covers a different real length | The graticule moves when the objective is changed | The stage micrometer shrinks at higher power | The eyepiece magnification changes with the objective | The graticule sits in the eyepiece, but each objective enlarges the specimen differently, so one division stands for a new real length.
M3@2: A student wants to show how cells are arranged across a whole onion epidermis. What should they draw? | A low-power plan showing the regions of tissue | A high-power drawing of a single cell's detail | A high-power drawing of every cell in the field | A low-power drawing with each nucleus shaded in | A low-power plan shows the layout of tissue regions; a high-power drawing is used for the detail inside one cell.
SUM: Prepare a thin, stained specimen under a gently lowered coverslip, and focus on low power with coarse then fine focus before moving to high power.
SUM: Total magnification is the eyepiece magnification multiplied by the objective magnification.
SUM: Every drawing needs full labels and a magnification scale; a low-power plan shows tissue regions and a high-power drawing shows one cell.
SUM: An eyepiece graticule must be calibrated against a stage micrometer for each objective before it can measure cells.
